title: Gradient Boosting vs. Neural Networks: When Classical ML Still Wins
excerpt: A deep-dive into why gradient-boosted trees consistently outperform deep learning on tabular data, and how to decide which paradigm to deploy in production.
content:
The Tabular-Data Paradox

Deep learning has conquered images, text, and audio—yet on structured, tabular datasets the leaderboard is still dominated by XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost. In Kaggle competitions from 2019 to 2025, gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) won over 70 % of tabular challenges. Why?

1. Inductive Bias and Feature Interactions

Neural networks learn representations through continuous, differentiable functions. GBDTs, on the other hand, partition feature space with axis-aligned splits. For data that already arrives as hand-crafted numeric and categorical columns—credit scores, sensor readings, transaction logs—those splits map naturally onto the data's decision boundaries.

Consider a fraud-detection table with columns like transaction_amount, merchant_category, and time_since_last_txn. A single tree split on transaction_amount > 5000 immediately captures an important boundary. A neural network would need to learn this threshold implicitly through back-propagation across many mini-batches.

2. Handling Heterogeneous Features

Real-world tables mix continuous features (salary, age), ordinal features (education level), and high-cardinality categoricals (zip code, product SKU). GBDTs natively handle missing values—XGBoost learns a default direction for NaN splits—while neural nets require imputation, embedding layers, and careful normalisation.

CatBoost introduced ordered target encoding that avoids data leakage when encoding categoricals, an issue neural-net pipelines often overlook.

3. Sample Efficiency

Modern tabular datasets in production are large but not ImageNet-scale. With 10 k–500 k rows, GBDTs converge faster than neural networks and generalise better without the heavy regularisation (dropout, weight decay, data augmentation) that deep models require.

4. When Neural Nets Actually Help

  • Multi-modal inputs — If your table includes a free-text column or an image URL, a transformer or CNN sub-network can extract features that are then concatenated with tabular features.
  • Massive scale — Google's Wide & Deep model showed that when you have billions of rows, neural nets can capture long-tail interactions that trees miss.
  • Transfer learning — Pre-trained tabular foundation models (e.g., TabPFN, SAINT) are an active area of research, potentially closing the gap.

5. Practical Decision Framework

FactorPrefer GBDTPrefer DL
Dataset size< 500 k rows> 5 M rows
Feature typesAll numeric / low-card catMixed with text/images
Interpretability needHigh (SHAP, feature importance)Low
Training budgetCPU, minutesGPU, hours

Conclusion

Don't reach for a neural network out of habit. Profile your data, benchmark a GBDT baseline in under an hour, and only escalate to deep learning when the evidence justifies the complexity. Classical ML isn't going anywhere—it's battle-tested, interpretable, and remarkably hard to beat on the right problems.
author: Debnil Pal

title: Attention Is All You Need — But Tokenization Is All You Forget
excerpt: Exploring how tokenization strategies—BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece, and byte-level—silently shape every NLP model's performance, and practical tips for choosing the right one.
content:
Why Tokenization Matters More Than You Think

Every transformer-based NLP pipeline starts with a tokenizer, yet it's the component engineers spend the least time tuning. The tokenizer converts raw text into integer IDs that the model actually sees. A poor tokenizer creates longer sequences, wastes context window, and introduces artificial word boundaries that confuse downstream tasks.

1. Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)

BPE, introduced by Sennrich et al. (2016), iteratively merges the most frequent pair of adjacent tokens. GPT-2 and GPT-3 use BPE with a vocabulary of ~50 k merges.

Strength: Elegant balance between character-level and word-level. Rare words decompose into recognisable sub-words (unhappiness → un + happiness).

Weakness: Merge order is deterministic, so the same word always splits the same way—no stochastic regularisation. Also, it's language-agnostic but trained predominantly on English corpora, causing poor splits for agglutinative languages like Turkish or Finnish.

2. WordPiece

Used by BERT and its descendants, WordPiece is similar to BPE but selects merges that maximise the likelihood of the training corpus under a unigram language model. The special ## prefix marks continuation sub-words.

Key difference from BPE: WordPiece optimises a probabilistic objective, while BPE uses raw frequency counts. In practice, the resulting vocabularies are similar for English, but WordPiece tends to produce slightly shorter sequences for scientific and medical text.

3. SentencePiece & Unigram Model

SentencePiece (Kudo & Richardson, 2018) treats the input as a raw byte stream—no pre-tokenization into words. This makes it truly language-agnostic. The unigram variant starts with a large vocabulary and prunes tokens that contribute least to the corpus likelihood.

T5, mT5, and LLaMA all use SentencePiece. For multilingual models, it's the de facto choice because it handles scripts without explicit word boundaries (Chinese, Japanese, Thai) gracefully.

4. Byte-Level Tokenization

Models like ByT5 and recent MegaByte architectures operate directly on UTF-8 bytes. No vocabulary at all—just 256 possible tokens.

Pros: Zero out-of-vocabulary issues; trivially handles any language, emoji, or code.

Cons: Sequences become 3–5× longer, increasing memory and compute quadratically for attention layers. Byte-level models compensate with local attention windows or patching (grouping bytes into fixed-length patches).

5. Practical Tips

  • Domain-specific re-training: If your corpus is heavy on code, chemical formulae, or legal jargon, re-train or extend the tokenizer vocabulary. A tokenizer that turns JavaScript into [Java, ##script] wastes a token on every mention.
  • Measure fertility: Fertility = average number of tokens per word. A fertility above 1.5 for your dominant language suggests the tokenizer needs more merges.
  • Pre-tokenization matters: Whitespace splitting, regex-based splitting (GPT-4 pattern), or no splitting (SentencePiece) all affect downstream quality. Test on your validation set.
  • Normalisation: Unicode NFKC normalisation before tokenization prevents duplicate tokens for visually identical characters (e.g., full-width vs. half-width katakana).

Conclusion

Tokenization is the unsung foundation of NLP. Before you tune hyperparameters or scale model size, audit your tokenizer. A well-chosen tokenization strategy can deliver gains equivalent to a 10–20 % increase in model parameters—at zero extra inference cost.
author: Debnil Pal

title: Residual Connections, Skip Paths, and the Geometry of Deep Networks
excerpt: Why residual connections are the single most important architectural innovation in deep learning, visualised through loss landscapes and gradient flow analysis.
content:
The Depth Problem

In 2015, Kaiming He's team at Microsoft Research showed something counter-intuitive: a 56-layer plain CNN performed worse than a 20-layer one on CIFAR-10. More layers should mean more capacity, so why did training accuracy degrade?

The answer wasn't overfitting—it was optimisation difficulty. Without residual connections, the loss landscape of deep networks becomes exponentially more chaotic as depth increases, creating saddle points and flat regions that stall gradient descent.

1. What Residual Connections Do

A residual block computes y = F(x) + x, where F is the learned transformation (e.g., two 3×3 conv layers). The + x identity shortcut means the block only needs to learn the residual—the difference from the input—rather than the full mapping.

Mathematically, this creates a gradient highway. During back-propagation, the gradient of the loss with respect to an early layer l in a network with L layers becomes:

∂L/∂x_l = ∂L/∂x_L · (1 + ∂/∂x_l Σ F_i)

The critical "1" term means the gradient always has a direct path back to early layers, even if the learned residual functions have near-zero gradients. This is why ResNets train smoothly at 100, 200, even 1000 layers.

2. Loss Landscape Visualisation

Li et al. (2018) visualised neural network loss landscapes by projecting the high-dimensional parameter space onto two random directions. Plain networks show sharp, chaotic surfaces full of local minima. ResNets show smooth, convex-like bowls—dramatically easier for SGD to navigate.

This smoothness isn't just aesthetic; it explains why ResNets are more robust to hyperparameter choices. You can train a ResNet-50 with a wide range of learning rates and batch sizes and still converge, whereas a 50-layer plain net requires meticulous tuning.

3. Beyond Vision: Residuals Everywhere

  • Transformers: Every transformer block is a residual block. Multi-head attention output is added to the input, and the feed-forward output is added to the attention output. Without these skips, transformer training collapses.
  • Diffusion models: U-Net architectures in Stable Diffusion and DALL-E use skip connections between encoder and decoder blocks at matching resolutions, preserving spatial detail.
  • Graph Neural Networks: GCN and GAT variants add residual connections to prevent over-smoothing—the phenomenon where node features converge to the same vector as depth increases.

4. Variants and Extensions

Pre-activation ResNets (He et al., 2016b) place batch normalisation and ReLU before the convolution, yielding y = x + F(BN(ReLU(x))). This further smooths the loss landscape and is the default in modern architectures.

Dense connections (DenseNet) concatenate all previous feature maps instead of adding them, providing even richer gradient flow but at higher memory cost.

Stochastic depth randomly drops entire residual blocks during training (replacing F(x) + x with just x), acting as a powerful regulariser and reducing training time by ~25 %.

5. Practical Implications

  • Always use skip connections when building networks deeper than ~8 layers.
  • For custom architectures, ensure dimension matching via 1×1 convolutions or linear projections on the shortcut path.
  • Monitor gradient norms per layer during training. If early-layer gradients are 100× smaller than late-layer gradients, your skip connections may be improperly configured.

Conclusion

Residual connections transformed deep learning from an art of careful initialisation and shallow architectures into an engineering discipline where depth is essentially free. Understanding why they work—gradient highways and smooth loss landscapes—makes you a better architect of any neural system.
author: Debnil Pal

title: Quantum Feature Maps: How Quantum Computing Reshapes Machine Learning Kernels
excerpt: An accessible introduction to Quantum Machine Learning, exploring how parameterised quantum circuits create exponentially rich feature spaces that classical kernels cannot efficiently replicate.
content:
Classical Kernels Hit a Wall

Kernel methods—SVMs, Gaussian processes, kernel PCA—work by implicitly mapping data into a high-dimensional feature space where linear separation becomes possible. The kernel trick lets us compute dot products in this space without ever materialising the features, keeping computation tractable.

But some feature spaces are so vast that even the kernel trick struggles. For problems with complex, entangled feature interactions—molecular property prediction, combinatorial optimisation, cryptographic analysis—classical kernels either under-fit or require exponential time to evaluate.

This is where quantum feature maps enter the picture.

1. What Is a Quantum Feature Map?

A quantum feature map φ(x) encodes a classical data point x into a quantum state |φ(x)⟩ on n qubits. The quantum state lives in a 2^n-dimensional Hilbert space—exponentially larger than what n classical features can span.

A typical encoding circuit:

  1. Apply Hadamard gates to all qubits (create superposition).
  2. Apply parameterised rotation gates R_z(x_i) encoding each feature into a qubit's phase.
  3. Apply entangling gates (CNOTs) to create correlations between qubits.
  4. Repeat layers for depth d.

The resulting quantum kernel is K(x, x') = |⟨φ(x)|φ(x')⟩|², computable by running both encoding circuits and measuring overlap (the swap test or compute-uncompute method).

2. Quantum Advantage in Kernel Space

Havlíček et al. (2019) proved that there exist quantum feature maps whose corresponding kernels are classically intractable—no polynomial-time classical algorithm can compute the same kernel function. This is a provable separation, not just a heuristic speedup.

In practice, the advantage depends on the data. For datasets whose structure aligns with the symmetries of the quantum circuit (e.g., periodic functions, group-theoretic patterns), quantum kernels can outperform RBF and polynomial kernels with far fewer support vectors.

3. Variational Quantum Classifiers

Instead of computing kernels explicitly, we can train a parameterised quantum circuit (PQC) end-to-end, analogous to a neural network:

  1. Encoding layer: Map classical features to quantum states.
  2. Variational layers: Apply trainable rotation and entangling gates.
  3. Measurement: Measure expectation values of Pauli operators.
  4. Classical optimiser: Use gradient-based (parameter shift rule) or gradient-free methods to minimise a loss function.

This approach, called a Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) when applied to chemistry or Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) for combinatorial problems, is the most near-term viable form of quantum ML.

4. Current Limitations

  • Noise: Today's quantum hardware (NISQ era) has gate error rates of ~0.1–1 %, limiting useful circuit depth to ~50–100 gates. Error mitigation techniques (zero-noise extrapolation, probabilistic error cancellation) help but add overhead.
  • Barren plateaus: Random PQCs suffer from exponentially vanishing gradients as qubit count increases—the quantum analogue of the vanishing gradient problem. Careful circuit architecture (local entanglement, symmetry-preserving ansätze) mitigates this.
  • Data loading bottleneck: Encoding N classical data points requires O(N) circuit executions, negating any quantum speedup for the encoding step itself.

5. Where QML Shows Real Promise

  • Drug discovery: Quantum circuits can natively simulate molecular Hamiltonians, making quantum kernels a natural fit for molecular property prediction.
  • Materials science: Predicting properties of quantum materials (superconductors, topological insulators) where the data itself is quantum in nature.
  • Anomaly detection: Quantum one-class SVMs can detect outliers in high-dimensional sensor data with provably richer decision boundaries.
  • Generative modelling: Quantum Born machines sample from probability distributions that are hard for classical models to represent, useful for financial simulation and synthetic data generation.

Getting Started

Frameworks like PennyLane (Xanadu), Qiskit Machine Learning (IBM), and Cirq + TensorFlow Quantum (Google) let you prototype quantum ML models on simulators and run them on real quantum hardware via cloud APIs. Start with a toy classification problem (e.g., the Iris dataset with 2 qubits) before scaling up.

Conclusion

Quantum Machine Learning is not a silver bullet, but it opens feature spaces that are genuinely inaccessible to classical methods. As hardware improves and error correction matures, quantum kernels and variational classifiers will become practical tools in the ML engineer's toolkit—especially for problems rooted in quantum physics itself.
author: Debnil Pal

title: ML-Powered Web: From Recommendation Engines to Real-Time Personalisation
excerpt: How machine learning is transforming modern web applications—from search ranking and content recommendations to on-device inference with TensorFlow.js and WebAssembly.
content:
The Invisible ML Layer of the Modern Web

Every time you open Netflix, scroll Twitter, or search on Google, dozens of ML models fire in the background—ranking results, filtering spam, personalising ads, and predicting your next click. Machine learning is no longer a back-office analytics tool; it's a core component of web architecture.

1. Recommendation Engines

Recommendation systems are the most impactful ML application on the web. They drive ~35 % of Amazon's revenue, 80 % of Netflix views, and most of YouTube's watch time.

Collaborative filtering finds users similar to you and recommends what they liked. Content-based filtering analyses item features (genre, description, tags) to match your preferences. Modern systems combine both via hybrid models.

The state of the art uses deep learning embeddings: users and items are mapped into a shared vector space where proximity indicates relevance. Two-tower models (one tower for user features, one for item features) enable real-time candidate retrieval at scale. YouTube's recommendation system uses a two-tower architecture to narrow billions of videos to ~1000 candidates in under 10 ms.

2. Search Ranking with Learning to Rank

Traditional search engines used TF-IDF and BM25 for document retrieval. Modern web search layers ML on top:

  • Stage 1 — Retrieval: Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) search over dense embeddings (produced by BERT-like models) retrieves the top 1000 candidates.
  • Stage 2 — Ranking: A cross-encoder model scores each (query, document) pair for fine-grained relevance. This is expensive, so it only runs on the shortlist.
  • Stage 3 — Re-ranking: Business rules, diversity constraints, and freshness signals adjust the final order.

Tools like Elasticsearch now support dense vector search natively, and libraries like FAISS and ScaNN handle billion-scale ANN retrieval.

3. Real-Time Personalisation

Web applications increasingly adapt in real time. E-commerce sites change product layouts, pricing displays, and promotional banners based on ML predictions about user intent.

Contextual bandits (e.g., LinUCB) balance exploration and exploitation: show a new banner to some users (explore), measure click-through rate, and shift traffic to the winner (exploit). This is faster than A/B testing because it adapts continuously.

Feature stores (Feast, Tecton) serve pre-computed user features (session count, purchase history, device type) to ML models at inference time with sub-millisecond latency, enabling real-time decisions.

4. On-Device ML with TensorFlow.js and WebAssembly

Not all ML needs a server round-trip. TensorFlow.js runs trained models directly in the browser using WebGL for GPU acceleration. Use cases:

  • Pose estimation (MoveNet) for fitness apps — no video leaves the user's device.
  • Text toxicity detection for comment moderation — instant feedback before submission.
  • Image classification for accessibility — describe photos for visually impaired users.

ONNX Runtime Web and WebAssembly (WASM) provide another path: compile models to WASM for near-native speed without GPU dependency. This is ideal for CPU-bound tasks like tabular inference (e.g., a risk score computed client-side).

5. Practical Architecture for ML-Powered Web Apps

A typical production setup:

  1. Training pipeline: Train models offline in Python (PyTorch/TF) on historical data. Export to ONNX or SavedModel format.
  2. Model serving: Deploy via TensorFlow Serving, Triton Inference Server, or a simple FastAPI wrapper behind a load balancer.
  3. Feature pipeline: Streaming features from Kafka → Flink → Feature Store. Batch features via Spark → S3 → Feature Store.
  4. API gateway: The web backend calls the model service, merges predictions with business logic, and returns JSON to the frontend.
  5. Monitoring: Track prediction drift (population stability index), latency (p99), and business KPIs (CTR, conversion) in Grafana.

6. Emerging Trends

  • LLM-powered search: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines vector search with language model synthesis for conversational web search.
  • Edge ML: Cloudflare Workers AI and Vercel AI SDK bring model inference to CDN edge nodes, reducing latency to <50 ms globally.
  • Federated learning: Train models across user devices without centralising data—Chrome's FLoC/Topics API (privacy-preserving ad targeting) is an early example.

Conclusion

Machine learning is now inseparable from web technology. Whether you're building a content platform, an e-commerce store, or a SaaS dashboard, understanding how to integrate ML into your web stack—from server-side serving to client-side inference—is a critical skill for modern developers.
author: Debnil Pal
